title: Jupiter: A Journey to the King of the Planets

lines: There is a planet so big that more than thirteen hundred Earths could fit inside it.
It has a storm wider than our whole world, winds faster than any hurricane, and lightning flashing deep in its clouds.
It has no solid ground to stand on, a magnetic field stronger than any other planet's, and radiation that would kill a person many times over.
And it is orbited by more than ninety moons, including one with hundreds of active volcanoes, and others that may hide oceans under their ice.
This is Jupiter, the king of the planets.
So today, let's take a proper tour of the biggest world in our solar system.
Jupiter is about one hundred forty three thousand kilometres wide at its equator.
That's roughly eleven times the width of Earth.
If Jupiter were a hollow ball, you could pour about one thousand three hundred twenty Earths inside it.
It is also heavy. Jupiter has about three hundred eighteen times the mass of Earth.
In fact, it has more than twice the mass of all the other planets in the solar system put together.
But for all that mass, Jupiter is not very dense.
Its average density is only about a quarter of Earth's, because it is made mostly of the two lightest elements, hydrogen and helium.
By number of molecules, its atmosphere is about ninety percent hydrogen and ten percent helium, with traces of methane, ammonia and water.
That's a recipe a lot like the Sun's, which is why Jupiter is sometimes called a failed star.
It isn't really. To start fusing hydrogen like a star, Jupiter would need about eighty times more mass than it has.

chapters.name: A fast spin, a long year

lines: Jupiter orbits the Sun about five point two times farther out than Earth does, roughly seven hundred seventy eight million kilometres away.
Out there, one trip around the Sun takes almost twelve Earth years.
So if you were ten years old in Jupiter years, you'd be well over a hundred in Earth years.
Yet Jupiter spins faster than any other planet.
A day on Jupiter lasts just under ten hours.
That fast spin squashes the planet a little, so it bulges at the equator and looks slightly flattened at the poles.
It also stretches the clouds into the famous stripes.
The pale stripes are called zones, and the darker ones are called belts.
Winds race along them in opposite directions, in places faster than five hundred kilometres per hour.
What we see on Jupiter is only the top of its clouds.
Scientists think there are three main cloud decks: ammonia ice at the top, then ammonium hydrosulfide, and water ice deeper down.
At the cloud tops, the temperature is around minus one hundred ten degrees Celsius.
But it gets warmer as you sink. At about ten times Earth's surface pressure, the air is roughly room temperature.
Spacecraft have seen lightning flashing in these clouds, first spotted by Voyager in nineteen seventy nine.
And then there is the Great Red Spot.
It's a giant storm, spinning counterclockwise in Jupiter's southern hemisphere.
Winds at its edge reach around six hundred eighty kilometres per hour, over three times faster than the strongest hurricanes on Earth.
Astronomers have watched it since at least the eighteen hundreds, and it may be the same storm first seen in the sixteen hundreds.
Today it is about sixteen thousand kilometres across, around one point three times the width of Earth.
That sounds huge, but it used to be much bigger. Over the last century and a half, the Great Red Spot has been shrinking.
Nobody knows for sure why it is red, or whether it will one day disappear.
The poles are just as strange.
When NASA's Juno spacecraft reached Jupiter in twenty sixteen, it became the first to get a clear look at them.
At the north pole, a giant cyclone sits in the middle, ringed by eight more cyclones, arranged almost like petals on a flower.
The south pole has its own ring of cyclones too.
Juno also found that Jupiter's stripes and storms don't just sit on top. They reach deep down into the planet.
So what would happen if you tried to land on Jupiter?
You couldn't. Jupiter has no solid surface.
As you fall, the gas around you gets thicker and hotter, and slowly turns into something more like a liquid.
Deeper still, the pressure is so extreme that hydrogen is squeezed into a strange form called metallic hydrogen, which can carry electricity.
At the very centre, scientists used to picture a small, solid core.
But Juno's measurements of Jupiter's gravity suggest the core may be fuzzy, large and partly dissolved into the layers above it.
Some researchers even think it might rain diamonds somewhere deep inside, though no one has proven it.
Jupiter is also still releasing heat left over from its formation.
It gives off more heat than it receives from the Sun.
Scientists think Jupiter was probably the first planet to form, around four and a half billion years ago.
Some models even suggest it drifted inward toward the Sun and then back out again, shaping the solar system as it moved.
All that metallic hydrogen, spinning quickly, creates the strongest magnetic field of any planet.
It was first detected up close by Pioneer ten in nineteen seventy three.
Jupiter's magnetic bubble, called the magnetosphere, is enormous.
On the side facing the Sun, it can stretch up to three million kilometres out.
Behind the planet, it trails away for up to a billion kilometres, reaching all the way toward the orbit of Saturn.
scenes.callout: Strongest magnetic field of any planet

lines: Trapped in that field are belts of charged particles.
The radiation around Jupiter is more than a thousand times the dose that would kill a human.
It can damage even shielded spacecraft, which is why Juno keeps its most important electronics inside a titanium vault.
Where those particles crash into Jupiter's atmosphere near the poles, they light up glowing auroras.
They are some of the most spectacular auroras in the whole solar system.
Here's something many people don't know: Jupiter has rings.
They are faint and dark, nothing like Saturn's, and they were only discovered by Voyager one in nineteen seventy nine.
They're made of fine dust, knocked off Jupiter's small inner moons by tiny meteor impacts.
Jupiter's moons have a famous history.
In sixteen ten, Galileo Galilei pointed one of his early telescopes at Jupiter and saw four little points of light next to it.
Night after night, they moved, always staying close to the planet.
Galileo realised they were circling Jupiter.
It was strong evidence that not everything in the sky goes around the Earth.
Today these four are called the Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
Jupiter has more than ninety known moons in total, and astronomers keep finding more small ones.
But the four big ones are worlds in their own right.
Io is the most volcanically active world we know.
It has more than four hundred active volcanoes, some of them throwing plumes high above the surface.
Io is squeezed and stretched by Jupiter's gravity as it orbits, and that constant flexing heats its insides.
Its solid surface rises and falls by around a hundred metres, like a tide made of rock.
Europa, the smallest of the four, is covered in a shell of ice.
Beneath that ice, scientists are confident there is a salty ocean of liquid water.
It may hold about twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans combined.
There are even hints of water vapour plumes escaping into space.
That makes Europa one of the best places in the solar system to look for conditions that could support life.
Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system.
At about five thousand two hundred sixty kilometres across, it is bigger than the planet Mercury.
It is also the only moon known to have its own magnetic field, and it probably has an ocean buried between layers of ice.
Callisto is the third largest moon in the solar system, and one of the most heavily cratered objects we know.
Its old, dark surface has barely changed in billions of years.
Even so, there is evidence that Callisto may hide an ocean too.
We have been visiting Jupiter for more than fifty years.
Pioneer ten made the first flyby in December nineteen seventy three, followed by Pioneer eleven a year later.
In nineteen seventy nine, the two Voyager spacecraft swept past, discovering the rings and Io's volcanoes.
Later, Ulysses, Cassini and New Horizons all flew by on their way to somewhere else.
The first spacecraft to orbit Jupiter was Galileo, which arrived in December nineteen ninety five.
It dropped a small probe straight into the atmosphere.
The probe fell about one hundred fifty kilometres into the clouds, sending back data for nearly an hour before it was destroyed.
Galileo itself studied Jupiter and its moons until twenty oh three.
Then NASA steered it into Jupiter on purpose, so it could never crash into Europa and contaminate a possible ocean.
Jupiter also gave us a front row seat to a cosmic collision.
In July nineteen ninety four, comet Shoemaker Levy nine, already broken into more than twenty pieces, slammed into Jupiter one after another.
The Hubble Space Telescope and the Galileo spacecraft watched as the impacts left dark scars in the clouds, some about as wide as Earth.
Jupiter's huge gravity is often said to protect Earth by catching or flinging away comets like this one.
But scientists point out it's a mixed blessing, because Jupiter can also nudge objects toward the inner planets.
The next chapter has already launched.
Europe's Juice mission left Earth in April twenty twenty three and is expected to arrive in twenty thirty one.
After flying past Europa and Callisto, it will go into orbit around Ganymede.
NASA's Europa Clipper launched in October twenty twenty four and should reach Jupiter in twenty thirty, to study whether Europa's ocean could be habitable.
Next time you look up on a clear night, look for a bright, steady point of light.
Often, only the Moon and Venus outshine Jupiter in the night sky.
Even a pair of binoculars can show you the same four moons Galileo saw more than four hundred years ago.
Jupiter is a giant storm, a magnetic monster, and a mini solar system all at once.
Which of Jupiter's moons would you want to explore first: fiery Io, icy Europa, giant Ganymede, or ancient Callisto?
Tell me in the comments, and subscribe for more journeys across the solar system.

description:
Jupiter is so big that 1,321 Earths could fit inside it. In this full tour of the king of the planets we cover its size and mass, why it is not really a failed star, its 10-hour day, the zones, belts and 500+ km/h winds, the shrinking Great Red Spot, Juno's polar cyclones, the metallic hydrogen and fuzzy core inside, the strongest magnetic field of any planet and its deadly radiation, the faint rings, Galileo's 1610 discovery, the Galilean moons Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, every mission from Pioneer 10 to Juno, comet Shoemaker-Levy 9, and the Juice and Europa Clipper missions on their way.

All visuals are original computer-generated renders (not real photographs). Narration is AI-generated.

Sources: ESA Facts about Jupiter (esa.int); Space.com Jupiter guide; The Planetary Society, Jupiter; BBC Sky at Night Magazine, 43 facts about Jupiter; NASA JPL Great Red Spot release (2019); Astronomy.com and Sky & Telescope (shrinking Great Red Spot).
